component.name: Trace Commons
component.summary: Review and contribute your coding sessions

description.p: Trace Commons contributes the sessions you have with coding agents to an open corpus, with your explicit consent for each one. Nothing leaves your machine until you have seen exactly what it contains.
The application watches the session folders you nominate, and nothing else. It will not guess: until you say which folders to watch, it watches none of them.
Every session is scanned for secrets and personal information and shown to you in full before anything is sent. You decide per session, or arm a project you trust to contribute without asking.
Choose GitHub, Google or a NEAR wallet when signing in to NEAR AI. Wallet sign-in requests a login message, not a transaction.
Open Cloud billing for the organization associated with your inference key, with an account check before opening the browser.
Tool cards and account sign-in explanations are clearer across the desktop apps.
Route AI requests through NEAR AI. Private AI now starts with sign-in when you are signed out, with clearer controls and status messages across Linux, macOS and Windows.
Private AI keys, Commons sessions and device keys now use the operating system credential store. Existing credentials migrate automatically when read, preserving your device identity.
Wallet signup now checks that the server is ready and explains mismatched signup details before signing a device proof.

Every session in the list now says whether it carries a checkable copy of the model call that produced it. That is a statement about the recording, not about your standing, so it is on every row for every contributor, including those who already have an invite and whose sessions send perfectly well. A session can arrive without such a copy whichever of those you are, and until now there was no way to tell which of yours had one.

Where a session has no usable copy, the row says which fact is in the way. Most of those cannot be changed afterwards, because they are about bytes that were already sent. One names a setting, because it is the only case where changing something helps the sessions you record next. One is neither: if the service that issues the receipt could not be reached, the session is not marked as lacking proof, but as unknown, and the row says the receipt could not be fetched. An unreachable service is not evidence about your session, and it may well succeed later. There is nothing to press here; the mark describes the recording and offers no button that would imply otherwise.

Separately, each session can also say whether you are allowed to send it at all, and which of its own facts stands in the way when you are not. That is the other question -- whether you may send this session, rather than whether its record is complete. Contributing without an invite is switched on in this release: a contribution is admitted on evidence it carries rather than on someone vouching for you, and you join with the NEAR AI login you already have rather than a wallet. An invited contributor sees no such line, because every one of their sessions is contributable and that is the correct answer.
Approving a group sends the ones that may be sent and tells you how many it left behind. A group control that would send nothing is not offered.

OpenCode sessions are read, where OpenCode has been asked to export them. Only an export it was explicitly told to write is imported; nothing is taken from its working files. A session recorded in a format this version does not understand says so rather than being skipped in silence.

Signing in for Private AI can now be reached from the app. The sentence in front of the button says what pressing it does before you press it: it opens a browser, signs you in to a company that is not this app, and mints a key this app then keeps. Signing out removes the key from this computer and nothing else -- it does not revoke anything at the other end, and the screen says so.
A sign-in that is under way can be cancelled, and cancelling stops the attempt this computer is running rather than leaving it to time out.

Answering model calls on this computer now has its own screen, called Private AI, rather than a setting buried under Tools. It lists the coding tools on this computer and says, for each one, whether it is connected, whether anything has arrived from it, and whether it is actually answering. A settings file with the right value in it only proves a file has a value in it; until now there was no way to tell whether a single call had ever come through.

Connecting a tool is one decision at a time, behind a preview. The app shows the exact change it would make to that tool's own settings file and writes nothing until you say so. If you had already chosen something yourself, it says so and leaves it alone rather than replacing it.

The switch is also in the tray, the menu bar on macOS, and on a keyboard shortcut. Turning it off acts at once, because that only reduces what this computer will answer. Turning it on opens the screen first: while it is on, anything else running here can send calls through it, charged to the accounts you have set up, and that is worth deciding with the consequence in front of you.

The screen also says what the calls answered on this computer have cost. Only calls answered here are in that figure. Calls answered on another machine or in a browser are not, and neither is work a monthly plan has already paid for.

Two coding tools are supported, not four. One cannot be described because the app can write one of two request shapes and neither is that tool's; the other keeps no settings file that can be found. Saying so is better than implying more is on the way.

Despite the name, this screen promises no privacy of its own. Whatever confidentiality your calls have comes from wherever they are answered. What changes here is that the record is on your computer and the choice of who answers is yours.
The sidebar is now in the same order on Linux, macOS and Windows. Settings is last on all three; it used to sit in the middle on macOS, leaving two destinations below it.

On first start the app now asks once whether to answer model calls on this computer. It says plainly what that costs before you answer: while it is on, anything else running on this computer can send calls through it as well, charged to the accounts you have set up here, and on a shared machine that is anyone who can log in. It is off until you say yes, declining is remembered rather than asked again, and the setting stays where you can find it afterwards.

When it is on, the app says what it is actually doing rather than assuming. It distinguishes running, running with nothing to answer with, stopping, another copy of this app holding the setup, and a failure that will not clear until you turn the setting off and on again. Where it cannot tell, it says so instead of showing a state it did not check.

The sentences shown before you approve a session are now written once and read by every version of this app, so the Linux, macOS and Windows versions say the same thing about what leaves your machine. They had drifted apart.
A control that fails now says so. Where a setting could previously be left showing the value you chose after the app failed to save it, the app now reads back what was actually stored and shows that.

A new Tools section can read a record kept on this machine of where each of your tools sends its requests first, and says so one tool at a time: Private, Sends direct, Not known, or Not used. It is off until you turn it on, and changes apply straight away. On a machine already keeping such a record the port is found for you rather than asked for. It says where a request goes first and nothing about what happens to it afterwards, and where it does not know it says so rather than guessing.

The queue is now organised by the folder each session was worked in, rather than one long list. Open a folder to see its sessions. The folder is shown the way your disk spells it, so a project called IronWire is no longer flattened to ironwire.

The scrubbing panel now tells you two things where it used to tell you one. It has always said what was removed. It now says separately when something it recognised as a secret is still present in what would be sent, and it no longer counts such a value among the ones it took out. That was the wrong way round, on the one screen where you decide whether to send.
Where something is still present, the sentence says how many places it was found in, not how many secrets there are: one place can hold more than one value. Read it as at least this many.

You can also search the session as it was originally recorded, not only the scrubbed copy, to check whether a value you are worried about is really gone. If that check cannot run, the app says so rather than showing a clear result it did not verify.
A project set to contribute automatically now waits a day after you last work on a session before sending it. Arming no longer means the next thing you type leaves immediately.

When you mark a session as failed or partly successful, you can now add a short written note saying what went wrong. Writing one is optional and skipping it changes nothing. Nothing else in a trace can carry that: the transcript records what the agent did, not what you expected it to do instead.

The note is stored exactly as you write it. This is the one exception to the redaction that covers everything else -- file paths and email addresses elsewhere in a session are replaced with placeholders before upload, and replacing them in a note would remove the explanation it exists to give. Treat it as writing about your own work, and leave out anything you would not want in the corpus.
One protection still applies. If a note appears to contain a credential, the upload is refused and you are asked to remove it rather than having it quietly masked, so you know to change the key.

When you approve a session, the app now asks whether it did what you asked: worked, partly, or failed. Nothing in a transcript answers that question. An agent that stops has not thereby succeeded, and a run that recorded no error has not thereby done the job, so you are asked rather than guessed at.

Answering is optional and never blocks approving. Skipping is a normal answer -- the session is recorded as unknown, which is what every session before this release recorded. The question appears on the preview sheet, and each project group offers the same three answers for sending everything it has waiting at once.

The answer records whether the task was finished, and nothing else. It is not a rating: a run can finish the job by a route you disliked, or fail while doing the right thing, and those are a different question this does not ask. Your answer is not part of the preview shown above it, and the preview says so.

Nothing in the Linux app has changed in this release. It fixes the macOS app, where finishing setup could leave you looking at the last screen of it forever: the button that ends setup recorded that you were finished but did not move you on, so the app sat there as though the button had not been pressed. Every platform is published at one version number, so this one exists on Linux with nothing behind it.

You can now turn down a whole project from the waiting list itself. Each project already offered a way to send everything it had waiting; there was no way to say the opposite without going to Settings and finding the project in a list. The waiting list now offers both, and asks you to confirm, telling you how many traces it is about to clear.

Turning a project down also does what it says. Until now it stopped future sessions being offered but left everything already waiting sitting in the list, so the traces you had just declined stayed on screen. They are now cleared, and anything you had already approved is still sent -- a decision you have already made is not taken back by a preference you set afterwards.
The choice remains reversible. Setting the project back to being offered brings its waiting sessions back, including finished ones whose files will never change again.

Declining a trace now sticks. Choosing "Not this one" used to set aside only the exact conversation as it stood at that moment, so the moment you typed another message the same conversation came back to the waiting list, and it kept coming back for as long as you kept working in it. A declined conversation is now left alone for good, and in projects set to send automatically it is no longer picked up on your behalf after you have said no.

Cards are honest about what they cover. A very large conversation has its biggest delegated transcripts left out to keep it within its size limit, and the card now says so instead of describing a trimmed conversation as though it were whole. The conversation itself is never trimmed.

Traces that cannot be sent no longer wait forever. One too large to send is now recorded as refused when you approve it, rather than staying in the list offering a choice that could never succeed. A session the app cannot read at all is reported instead of quietly disappearing.

The app now costs almost nothing when it has nothing to do. It was re-reading and re-hashing every waiting session on every check, including the ones it had no room to offer you, which kept a processor core busy continuously and read gigabytes a minute to no purpose. It also no longer rewrites its records when nothing has changed.

Privacy risk is also labelled more honestly. A trace where the scrubber found a secret and removed it was being marked high risk, which described the scrubber working rather than anything left behind, and held those traces back from being accepted. High is now reserved for content redaction did not resolve. A privacy filter that could not examine the text is treated as high risk rather than as clean.

The watcher no longer re-reads and re-hashes every waiting session on every poll, so the app stops working when there is nothing to do. The daily upload budget can be changed without editing a file, and the app says when uploads are waiting on it.
The history screen now updates when a submission lands, instead of showing the counts it had at launch.

The queue no longer builds a preview for every waiting session at once, so opening the app does not pin the machine. Large sessions render without freezing, and queue rows are created as they scroll into view.
Submit a trace from the queue row, or every trace in a project, without opening the preview first. Opening a very large session no longer freezes the window.
Submit a trace straight from the queue, or every trace in a project, without opening the preview first. Session scanning now streams files instead of reading them whole.
